questions.text: AI only arrived in education recently, with the release of tools like ChatGPT.
questions.explanation: AI was already in schools through spell-checkers, recommendation systems, translation tools and adaptive learning platforms — what changed recently is that AI became visible.

questions.text: Which application does the lesson describe as the most mature use of AI in education?
questions.explanation: Adaptive learning platforms have been in use for years and are called the most mature application of AI in education — effective when they supplement, rather than replace, teacher-led instruction.

questions.text: Which limitations does the lesson attribute to automated assessment?

options.text: It cannot assess creativity or originality.
It cannot evaluate the quality of a student's thinking — only whether the output matches expected patterns.
It cannot replace the professional judgement of a teacher who knows their students.

questions.explanation: Grading multiple-choice tests and flagging plagiarism are listed among the things automated assessment does well; creativity, quality of thinking and professional judgement are what it cannot reach.

questions.text: What does the lesson recommend as a starting point for a teacher new to AI?

options.text: Replace a whole unit of the curriculum with AI-generated materials.
Choose one routine task, try AI for it, and evaluate the result honestly.
Wait until the school adopts an official AI platform.
Study prompt-engineering theory before touching any tool.

questions.explanation: The lesson's first practical suggestion is to try a single time-consuming routine task with AI and then judge honestly whether the result was useful and where it needed improvement.
